G-DPA_1.title: Data Processing Agreements
G-DPA_1.description: Use only processors that provide sufficient guarantees of appropriate technical and organisational measures (Art. 28(1)), and have a processing agreement with each one in writing, which may be electronic (Art. 28(9)). Art. 28(3) requires the contract to set out the subject-matter and duration of the processing, its nature and purpose, the type of personal data, the categories of data subjects and the obligations and rights of the controller, before it reaches the eight clauses in points (a) to (h). Recommendation: keep every processor in one list with its agreement, so none is missed.

G-DPA_2.title: Sub-processor Authorisation
G-DPA_2.description: A processor engages another processor only with the controller's prior specific or general written authorisation. Under a general authorisation the processor tells the controller in advance of each sub-processor it intends to add or replace, so that the controller can object (Art. 28(2)). The contract binds the processor to respect that rule and to impose the same data protection obligations on any sub-processor (Art. 28(3)(d), referring to Art. 28(2) and (4)). Recommendation: keep each processor's sub-processors, and your authorisation, with its agreement.

G-ROP_1.title: Records of Processing Activities
G-ROP_1.description: Record each processing activity with the seven Art. 30(1) entries: the name and contact details of the controller and, where applicable, the joint controller, the controller's representative and the data protection officer; purposes; categories of data subjects and of personal data; recipient categories; transfers to a third country or an international organisation, naming it, and for transfers under the second subparagraph of Art. 49(1) the documentation of suitable safeguards; and, where possible, erasure periods and a description of the measures. Art. 30(5) exempts organisations employing fewer than 250 persons, but only where the processing is occasional, is unlikely to result in a risk to rights and freedoms, and involves no special categories or criminal conviction data. Regular personnel and payroll processing is not occasional, so in practice the record is still owed.

G-TOM_1.title: Technical and Organisational Measures
G-TOM_1.description: Implement measures that protect personal data at a level appropriate to the risk, and document them so that you can demonstrate them (Art. 5(2), 24(1)). Art. 32(1) names, as appropriate: pseudonymisation and encryption; lasting confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience; timely restoration after an incident; and a process for regularly testing, assessing and evaluating their effectiveness.

G-BRC_1.title: Personal Data Breach Response Process
G-BRC_1.description: Notify the supervisory authority of a personal data breach without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware of it (Art. 33(1)). Notification is not owed where the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, so that assessment is recorded either way. A filing made after 72 hours states the reasons for the delay. Recommendation: write down how a breach is assessed and who notifies, so the 72 hours hold.

G-BRC_2.title: Personal Data Breach Documentation
G-BRC_2.description: Document every personal data breach, notifiable or not: the facts relating to it, its effects and the remedial action taken, so that the supervisory authority can verify compliance (Art. 33(5)).

G-DSR_1.title: Data Subject Rights Workflow
G-DSR_1.description: Answer access, erasure, rectification, portability, restriction and objection requests without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt (Art. 12(3), Art. 15 to 22). Where the complexity and number of requests make it necessary, the period may be extended by two further months; the data subject is told of the extension and the reasons within the first month. If you do not act on a request, tell the data subject without delay and at the latest within one month why, and that they may complain to a supervisory authority and seek a judicial remedy (Art. 12(4)). For a German controller §34(1) BDSG removes the Art. 15 right of access in narrow cases, for example data kept only because statutory or by-law retention rules forbid erasing it, where answering would take disproportionate effort and technical and organisational measures exclude any other use, and §35 BDSG replaces Art. 17 erasure with restriction of processing where, in non-automated processing, erasure is impossible or disproportionately costly because of the way the data is stored and the data subject's interest in erasure is minor; never for data processed unlawfully. §34(2) BDSG requires the reasons for refusing access to be documented.

G-BRC_3.title: Communication to affected data subjects
G-BRC_3.description: Tell affected individuals without undue delay about a breach that is likely to result in a high risk to them (Art. 34(1)). Notifying the supervisory authority under Art. 33 does not discharge it. The communication describes the nature of the breach in clear and plain language and carries the information in Art. 33(3)(b) to (d) (Art. 34(2)). It is not required where the data was rendered unintelligible (for example by encryption), where subsequent measures ensure the high risk is no longer likely to materialise, or where the effort would be disproportionate, in which case a public communication or a similar measure that informs them equally effectively is required instead (Art. 34(3)). In Germany it is also not owed insofar as it would disclose information that must be kept secret by law or by its nature, in particular because of a third party's overriding legitimate interests, unless the data subjects' interests, in particular in view of threatened harm, outweigh the interest in secrecy (§29(1) sentences 3 and 4 BDSG).

G-DPO_1.title: Designate a data protection officer
G-DPO_1.description: Assess and document whether a data protection officer must be designated. The GDPR requires one for public bodies, and where the core activities consist of regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects on a large scale, or of processing special categories of data (Art. 9) or data on criminal convictions (Art. 10) on a large scale (Art. 37(1)). In Germany the duty also applies where, as a rule, at least 20 persons are constantly engaged in the automated processing of personal data (§38(1) BDSG), and regardless of headcount where processing is subject to a data protection impact assessment or personal data are processed commercially for transfer, anonymised transfer or market or opinion research. Position and tasks follow Art. 38 and 39 GDPR; where the designation is required, the DPO can be removed or dismissed only for good cause (§38(2) with §6(4) BDSG). The contact details must be published and communicated to the supervisory authority (Art. 37(7)).
